title: Harappan Steatite Stamp Seal with Single-Horned Beast ('Unicorn') and Cult Brazier
localName: Ekashringa (later Sanskrit epithet; undeciphered Indus script)
originLocation: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh (modern Pakistan)
medium: Carved and fired white-slipped steatite intaglio stamp seal
creator: Unknown Harappan master lapidary
repository: Musée national des arts asiatiques – Guimet, Paris (AO 21166)
anatomy: single forward-sweeping S-curved horn emerging from the brow
muscular bovine-antelope torso with hatched neck collar
long tufted bovine tail and cloven hooves
description: Carved in crisp intaglio into fired steatite beneath a register of undeciphered Indus script signs, this Mature Harappan stamp seal depicts the iconic single-horned bovine-antelope standing before a two-tiered ritual incense burner or cult standard. Appearing on over sixty percent of stamped glyptic seals from Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the profile beast represents an intentional mythical single-horned emblem rather than two overlapping horns, establishing South Asia's earliest sacred unicorn tradition.

title: The 'Pashupati' ('Lord of Beasts') Horned Anthropomorphic Deity Seal
originLocation: DK-G Area, Mohenjo-daro, Sindh (modern Pakistan)
medium: Carved and fired steatite stamp seal (Seal 420)
creator: Unknown Harappan glyptic carver
repository: National Museum, New Delhi
anatomy: sweeping water-buffalo horns crowning a central vegetal crest
polycephalic three-faced anthropomorphic head
bangle-clad arms resting on knees in heel-to-heel yogic posture
description: Excavated in 1928–1929 at Mohenjo-daro, this famed steatite seal portrays an ithyphallic three-faced, buffalo-horned figure seated in a heel-to-heel yogic posture on a low dais above two ibexes. Surrounded by an elephant, a leaping tiger, a rhinoceros, and a water buffalo beneath seven Indus script glyphs, the therianthropic 'Lord of Beasts' synthesizes human, bovine, and wild-animal sovereignty in Bronze Age urban religion.

title: Torana Architrave Relief of a Warrior Wrestling an Aquatic Makara
originLocation: Stupa No. 3, Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh, India
medium: Carved buff sandstone gateway (torana) relief
creator: Unknown Sanchi stone-carving guild
repository: In situ, Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh, India
anatomy: gaping crocodilian jaws lined with serrated teeth
upturned proboscis-like snout and bulging eyes
coiling scaled pisciform body terminating in a foliate fin-tail
description: On the sandstone gateway (torana) of Stupa No. 3 at Sanchi, a tunic-clad warrior grapples with the gaping crocodilian jaws of a colossal coiled Makara amidst lotus-filled waters. In early Indian Buddhist and Hindu cosmology, the amphibious Makara embodies both the fecund abundance and perilous untamed waters of rivers and oceans, serving as an auspicious threshold guardian on stupa gateways.

title: Rock-Cut Nāgarāja and Nāginī Ascending the Cleft in Descent of the Ganges
originLocation: Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), Tamil Nadu, India
medium: Monumental open-air granite cliff relief
creator: Pallava royal sculptors under Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla)
repository: In situ, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu, India
anatomy: regal human upper torsos with palms joined in anjali mudra
fanning multi-headed cobra hoods (seven-hooded king, three-hooded queen)
sinuous undulating serpent tails emerging from the water cleft
description: Carved directly into the central vertical fissure of Mamallapuram's immense granite boulder relief—where rainwater once cascaded from a summit cistern to enact the sacred river's descent—a seven-hooded Nāgarāja and his three-hooded Nāginī consort swim upward in reverent adoration. Combining graceful anthropomorphic upper bodies with powerful coiling serpent tails and flaring cobra hoods, these semi-divine subterranean water spirits sanctify the union of heaven, earth, and the underworld (Patala).

title: Monumental Kala ('Face of Glory') Portal Lintel at Candi Kalasan
originLocation: Candi Kalasan, Sleman, Yogyakarta, Java, Indonesia
medium: Carved volcanic andesite stone architectural relief with stucco traces
creator: Unknown Central Javanese Buddhist master sculptor
repository: In situ, Candi Kalasan, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
anatomy: jawless leonine-demonic upper maw baring curved fangs
bulging hypnotic eyes beneath foliate horn-brows
clawed hands grasping vegetal scrolls disgorged from the mouth
description: Crowning the southern sanctuary niche and doorway of Candi Kalasan—the earliest dated Buddhist temple in Central Java—this monumental andesite Kala head glares down with bulging eyes and a fanged, lower-jawless maw framed by exuberant lotus scrolls. Adapted from the Indian Kirtimukha ('Face of Glory') that devoured its own body at Shiva's command, the Javanese Kala swallows time and malevolent forces before they can cross the sacred temple threshold.

title: Wall Relief of Kinnara and Kinnari Flanking the Wish-Fulfilling Kalpataru Tree
originLocation: Candi Pawon (Borobudur Temple Compounds), Magelang, Central Java, Indonesia
medium: Carved volcanic andesite bas-relief panel
creator: Unknown Shailendra court sculptor
repository: In situ, Candi Pawon, Borobudur Complex, Central Java, Indonesia
anatomy: crowned, jewel-bedecked human heads and upper torsos
plumed avian wings and rounded feathered bird bodies
taloned bird legs flanking pots of overflowing jewels
description: Carved on the exterior wall of Candi Pawon along the processional axis to Borobudur, a male Kinnara and female Kinnari stand beneath a jewel-hung Kalpataru (wish-fulfilling tree) surrounded by hovering celestial Apsaras. Half-human and half-bird inhabitants of Mount Meru's paradise, the pair guard treasure jars overflowing with riches while embodying eternal conjugal devotion, celestial music, and Buddhist merit.

title: Andesite Makara Stairway Balustrade Guardian of the Shiva Temple
originLocation: Candi Siwa, Prambanan Temple Compounds, Yogyakarta, Java, Indonesia
medium: Carved volcanic andesite stone balustrade sculpture
creator: Unknown Mataram royal stone carvers
repository: In situ, Prambanan Temple Compounds, Central Java, Indonesia
anatomy: curling elephantine trunk topped with a lotus bud
wide fanged jaws housing a miniature guardian lion within the maw
ram-like scrolled horns behind round eyes
description: Terminating the steep staircase balustrades leading up into the central Shiva sanctuary at Prambanan, this volcanic stone Makara curls its elephantine proboscis upward to balance a lotus bud while revealing a small roaring lion seated inside its toothy jaws. Paired with an overarching Kala lintel at the top of the stairs to form the classic Indo-Javanese Kala-Makara frame, the aquatic composite bridges the earthly courtyard and the cosmic mountain of the gods.

title: Granite Nāgarāja Guardstone (Muragala) Framed by Makara Torana
originLocation: Anuradhapura region, Sri Lanka
medium: High-relief carved crystalline limestone / granite stele
creator: Unknown Sinhalese monastic sculptor
repository: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (IS.8-1966)
anatomy: tiered conical crown backed by a multi-headed cobra hood
graceful tribhanga princely body holding a blooming pot of plenty (punkalasa)
miniature Makara arch above and pot-bellied gana dwarf at the feet
description: Placed beside the moonstone threshold of a Sri Lankan Buddhist monastery entrance, this Anuradhapura-period guardstone (muragala) depicts a serpent-king (Nāgarāja) in princely regalia beneath a protective canopy of flared cobra hoods and a miniature Makara arch. Holding a sprouting vase of plenty (punkalasa) in one hand and a flowering branch in the other while trampling or subduing a dwarf yaksha spirit, the Nāga king promises rain, agricultural prosperity, and apotropaic protection to pilgrims.

title: Monumental Sandstone Garuda in Dynamic Koh Ker Style
originLocation: Prasat Thom complex, Koh Ker (Chok Gargyar), Preah Vihear, Cambodia
medium: Carved grey sandstone sculpture in the round
creator: Unknown Khmer royal sculptor under King Jayavarman IV
repository: National Museum of Cambodia, Phnom Penh
anatomy: fierce hooked raptor beak with bulging eyes and diademed crest
powerful muscular human torso and raised arms
spread feathered wings and taloned avian legs
description: Carved in the bold, kinetic sculptural idiom of Jayavarman IV's short-lived capital at Koh Ker, this monumental sandstone Garuda crouches with wings unfurled, fierce hooked beak agape, and muscular arms raised in triumphant power. As the solar eagle-man mount (vahana) of Vishnu and the sworn enemy of the serpentine Nāgas, Garuda served in Khmer imperial iconography as an emblem of royal celestial authority and victory over chaos.

title: Seven-Headed Nāga Causeway Balustrade at Angkor Wat
originLocation: Angkor Wat, Siem Reap, Cambodia
medium: Carved sandstone monumental balustrade sculpture
creator: Khmer imperial stone-carving workshops under King Suryavarman II
repository: In situ, Angkor Wat, Siem Reap, Cambodia
anatomy: fan-shaped aureole of seven crowned serpent heads
fanged open jaws and flame-like cranial crests
hundred-meter cylindrical scaled serpent body raised on stone blocks
description: Flanking the sandstone causeways across the vast moat of Angkor Wat, immense seven-headed Nāga balustrades rear their crowned cobra hoods into sculpted fans before stretching their scaled bodies toward the temple-mountain sanctuary. In Khmer state cosmology, these Nāga bridges materialize the rainbow linking the mortal realm to Mount Meru while evoking the cosmic serpent Vasuki used by gods and demons to churn the Ocean of Milk.

title: Ornate Soapstone Makara Frieze on the Plinth of Hoysaleswara Temple
originLocation: Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu, Karnataka, India
medium: Deeply undercut chloritic schist (soapstone) temple basement frieze
creator: Hoysala guild sculptors under King Vishnuvardhana and Ketamalla
repository: In situ, Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu, Karnataka, India
anatomy: crocodile jaws with curled elephantine snout and boar tusks
muscular leonine limbs and scaly porcine-aquatic torso
extravagant foliate peacock-plumage tail in lace-like openwork
description: Along the star-shaped Jagati plinth of the Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu, Hoysala sculptors exploited soft, fine-grained chloritic schist to transform the aquatic Makara into an encyclopedic terrestrial-marine chimera. Combining crocodile jaws, an elephant trunk, boar tusks, lion paws, a monkey's eyes, and a lush cascade of foliate peacock tail-feathers, the creature parades in a dedicated register symbolizing cosmic abundance beneath scenes from the Hindu epics.

title: Tháp Mắm Style Sandstone Dragon-Makara Stairway Balustrade
originLocation: Tháp Mắm, Bình Định Province, Vietnam
medium: Carved sandstone architectural corner sculpture
creator: Unknown Cham sculptor of the Vijaya period
repository: Musée national des arts asiatiques – Guimet, Paris
anatomy: upturned flame-crested elephantine proboscis and fanged draconic jaws
crowned serpent-warrior or dragon emerging from the open gullet
layered scale armor and stylized spiral mane curls
description: Excavated at the monumental Vijaya-period sanctuary of Tháp Mắm in central Vietnam, this sandstone corner piece fuses the Indian Hindu-Buddhist Makara with sinuous East and Southeast Asian draconic motifs. With its upturned trunk, scrolled eyebrows, and scaled neck disgorging a crowned dragon-serpent head, the sculpture exemplifies Champa's maritime synthesis of Indic temple iconography and regional dragon lore.

title: Imperial Stone Dragon (Rồng) Stairway Balustrade of Kính Thiên Palace
originLocation: Kính Thiên Palace Foundation, Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, Hanoi, Vietnam
dateDisplay: 1467 CE (reign of Emperor Lê Thánh Tông)
medium: Monolithic carved grey limestone stairway balustrade
creator: Imperial court stone-carvers of Đại Việt
repository: In situ, Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, Hanoi, Vietnam
anatomy: horned draconic head with flaming mane and grasping pearl in the jaws
undulating cloud-wreathed serpentine body descending the steps
five-clawed imperial talons gripping swirling clouds
description: Constructed in 1467 under Emperor Lê Thánh Tông for the audience terrace of Kính Thiên Palace at the heart of the Thăng Long Citadel, four monolithic limestone dragons (Rồng) surge headfirst down the ceremonial steps amidst carved thunderclouds. Bearing five-clawed imperial talons, wind-swept manes, and sacred pearls in their jaws, the dragons embody the Vietnamese sovereign's heaven-mandated authority as well as the rain-bringing lineage of Lạc Long Quân ('Dragon Lord of Lạc').

title: Monolithic Rearing Yali (Vyala) Musical Mandapa Pillars
originLocation: Vitthala Temple Complex, Hampi, Karnataka, India
medium: Monolithic carved granite composite temple pillars
creator: Vijayanagara imperial stone-carvers
repository: In situ, Vitthala Temple Complex, Group of Monuments at Hampi, Karnataka, India
anatomy: ferocious leonine body rearing high on muscular hind legs
snarling fanged head with bulging eyes and stylized mane
clawed forepaws trampling a miniature Makara or elephant below
description: Hewn from single blocks of Deccan granite at the Vitthala Temple in Hampi, rows of colossal rearing Yalis (also called Vyalas) project outward from composite pavilion piers, often carrying armed riders on their backs while crushing miniature elephants or Makaras underfoot. Revered in South Indian temple architecture as more powerful than both the lion and the war-elephant, the chimeric Yali physically and symbolically bears the weight of the sacred mandapa while warding off chaos.

title: Monolithic Ugra Narasimha Sheltered by the Seven-Headed Serpent Shesha
originLocation: Hampi, Vijayanagara, Karnataka, India
medium: Colossal monolithic granite boulder sculpture (6.7 meters high)
creator: Commissioned by a Brahmin priest Arya Krishna Bhatta under Emperor Krishnadevaraya
repository: In situ, Hampi, Karnataka, India
anatomy: wrathful roaring lion head with protruding eyes and stylized flame-mane
four-armed human torso seated in cross-legged yogapatta meditation strap
canopy of seven-hooded cosmic serpent Adi Shesha arching overhead
description: Commissioned in 1528 CE during the reign of Emperor Krishnadevaraya and carved in situ from a single colossal granite boulder standing 6.7 meters tall, this statue portrays Vishnu's fourth avatar, Narasimha—the man-lion who burst from a palace pillar at twilight to slay the demon king Hiranyakashipu, whom neither man nor beast could kill. Seated in yogic mastery upon the coils of the cosmic serpent Adi Shesha beneath a seven-headed cobra canopy (originally with his consort Lakshmi on his left thigh prior to 1565), the monument radiates awesome protective ferocity.

title: Ceiling Relief of the Two-Headed Gandaberunda Clutching Lions and Elephants
originLocation: Rameshwara Temple, Keladi, Shivamogga District, Karnataka, India
medium: Carved granite mandapa ceiling relief medallion
creator: Keladi Nayaka temple stone-carvers under Chowdappa and Sadashiva Nayaka
repository: In situ, Rameshwara Temple, Keladi, Karnataka, India
anatomy: two symmetrical eagle-like heads facing opposite directions
hooked beaks grasping roaring lions that in turn seize elephants
outspread wings and immense talons lifting war-elephants effortlessly
description: Carved onto the mandapa ceiling of the Rameshwara Temple at Keladi, the royal emblem of Karnataka's rulers—the bicephalic Gandaberunda—spreads its wings while clutching lions in its twin beaks and full-grown elephants in its talons. In Hindu mythology, Vishnu assumed this colossal two-headed bird form to counter Shiva's Sharabha and restore cosmic equilibrium, making the creature an enduring symbol of unmatched imperial might from the Chalukyas and Vijayanagara to the Keladi Nayakas and Mysore Wadiyars.

title: Rearing Gajavyala (Lion-Elephant Yali) Pillar in the Thousand-Pillar Hall
originLocation: Aayiram Kaal Mandapam (Thousand-Pillar Hall), Meenakshi Amman Temple, Madurai, Tamil Nadu, India
medium: Monolithic carved grey granite temple pillar
creator: Commissioned by Ariyanatha Mudaliar, prime minister of Viswanatha Nayak
repository: In situ, Meenakshi Amman Temple, Madurai, Tamil Nadu, India
anatomy: lion's snarling face fused with a long curling elephantine trunk and tusks
sinewy feline body rearing vertically on powerful hind claws
scrolling foliate tail and lotus pedestal base
description: Guarding the central aisle of the celebrated 985-column Aayiram Kaal Mandapam at Madurai's Meenakshi Amman Temple, this monolithic granite Gajavyala fuses the roaring head and agile torso of a lion with the curling proboscis and tusks of an elephant. Known in Tamil as Yazhi, such lion-elephant hybrids epitomize Nayak-period sculptural virtuosity, uniting the supreme predators and royal mounts of the Indian forest into an invincible guardian of the temple precinct.

title: Ibrahim Rides into Battle on a Chariot Drawn by Spotted Horned Devs (Hamzanama)
originLocation: Imperial Mughal Atelier, Fatehpur Sikri or Agra, India
medium: Opaque watercolor, ink, and gold on large-format cotton cloth
creator: Imperial Mughal workshop directed by Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad
repository: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin (CBL In 01.2)
anatomy: curved bovine-caprine horns and pointed animal ears
spotted feline-like pelt in pink, orange, and slate hues
fanged grimacing mouths, clawed feet, and short tails
description: Painted on monumental cotton cloth for Emperor Akbar's fourteen-volume illustrated epic Hamzanama, this dynamic battle folio shows Amir Hamza's son Ibrahim charging across the fray in a wheeled war-chariot harnessed to subdued giant Devs. Synthesizing Persianate demonology with vivid Indian colorism and expressive energy, the Mughal artists rendered the supernatural Devs with leopard-spotted hides, curving horns, fanged grins, and gold-bell collars.

title: The Flight of the Simurgh Over a Mountainous Wilderness
originLocation: Lahore, Mughal Empire (modern Pakistan)
medium: Opaque watercolor and gold on paper
creator: Attributed to Basawan
repository: Aga Khan Museum, Toronto (AKM128, formerly Sadruddin Aga Khan Collection)
anatomy: colossal predatory bird head with powerful hooked beak
variegated wings of immense span scattering startled beasts below
streaming iridescent tail-plumes trailing across craggy peaks
description: Attributed to Emperor Akbar's master painter Basawan, this dramatic miniature captures a gigantic Simurgh swooping over a turbulent landscape where terrified elephants, rhinoceroses, lions, and a mounted hero scatter in awe. Transforming the graceful ribbon-tailed phoenix of Timurid and Safavid painting into a viscerally plausible, awe-inspiring avian titan capable of carrying off elephants in Indo-Persian lore, Basawan merges Mughal naturalism with mythic grandeur.

title: Carved Wooden Nghê Sacred Lion-Dog Guardian of Lâu Thượng Communal House
originLocation: Lâu Thượng Communal House (Đình), Việt Trì, Phú Thọ Province, Vietnam
medium: Carved and lacquered jackfruit/hardwood architectural sculpture
creator: Unknown Red River Delta village master woodcarver
repository: Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts, Hanoi
anatomy: spirited canine torso combined with a leonine-draconic head
wide grinning fanged mouth, bulging eyes, and flame-curled mane
sinewy clawed paws and bushy upturned tail
description: Originally perched among the timber rafters of Lâu Thượng village communal house (đình) in Phú Thọ province, this expressive 17th-century wooden Nghê embodies Vietnam's distinctively indigenous guardian beast. Blending the loyal domestic village dog with the auspicious attributes of the celestial lion and dragon-qilin (Kỳ Lân), the Nghê scrutinizes visitors' hearts at temples, shrines, and communal halls to dispel deceit and malevolent spirits.

title: Newar Repoussé Gilt-Copper Kirtimukha (Chepu) Temple Tympanum
civilization: Malla / Early Shah Period (Kathmandu Valley, Nepal)
originLocation: Kathmandu Valley, Nepal
medium: Gilt-copper repoussé torana crown relief
creator: Newar Shakya or Tamrakar metalwork artisan
repository: Temple portal, Kathmandu Valley, Nepal
anatomy: fierce horned grotesque face with three glaring eyes
clawed hands gripping writhing Nāga serpents at the corners of the jaws
flaming aureole crowning a semicircular repoussé torana
description: Hammered in high-relief gilt copper by Newar metalworkers of the Kathmandu Valley, this apex tympanum figure—known locally as Chepu and derived from the pan-Indic Kirtimukha—crowns a sacred temple torana while biting and clutching writhing Nāgas in its clawed hands. In Newar Hindu and Vajrayana Buddhist legend, Chepu is the celestial elder brother of Garuda, immortalized above every sanctum doorway as the supreme guardian of truth and fearlessness.

title: Gilt-Copper Snow Lion (Sengge) Roof Guardian of the Jokhang Temple
originLocation: Jokhang Temple, Lhasa, Tibet
medium: Hammered and parcel-gilt copper alloy architectural sculpture
creator: Tibetan-Newar monastery metalworkers
repository: In situ, Golden Roof of the Jokhang Temple, Lhasa, Tibet
anatomy: exuberant curling mane, eyebrow scrolls, and tail tufts
wide roaring fanged jaws and alert round eyes
upright seated leonine posture guarding the monastic roofline
description: Standing sentinel high on the gilded roof terraces of Lhasa's sacred Jokhang Temple, this hammered copper Snow Lion (Gangs Sengge) turns its roaring face and tightly coiled flame-curls toward the surrounding Himalayan peaks. Revered across Tibet as the fearless sovereign of snow-clad mountains—traditionally depicted in thangka painting with a white coat and turquoise mane—the Snow Lion symbolizes primordial cheerfulness, unshakeable Buddhist dharma, and the throne of enlightened Buddhas.

title: Al-Buraq, the Winged Human-Headed Steed of the Prophet's Night Journey
civilization: Deccani Sultanate / Asaf Jahi School (Hyderabad, India)
originLocation: Hyderabad, Deccan, India
medium: Opaque watercolor and gold on paper
creator: Unknown Hyderabad court painter
repository: National Museum, New Delhi (Acc. No. 58.58/158)
anatomy: crowned female human head adorned with pearl and gold jewelry
dappled equine body fitted with an embroidered royal saddlecloth
feathered angel wings and fanned iridescent peacock tail (plus cobra-terminated tail)
description: Painted in Hyderabad during the late 18th century, this radiant Deccani miniature portrays Al-Buraq—the lightning-swift celestial mount that bore the Prophet Muhammad from Mecca to Jerusalem and up through the heavens during the Mi'raj (Night Journey). In the distinctive Indo-Islamic visual synthesis of the Deccan, Buraq combines a crowned, jewel-bedecked maiden's face, feathered wings, a dappled steed's body, an iridescent peacock fan, and a protective serpent-headed tail.

title: Gilt-Bronze Kinnorn (Kinnara) Terrace Guardian at Wat Phra Kaew
originLocation: Upper Terrace around Phra Mondop, Wat Phra Kaew (Temple of the Emerald Buddha), Grand Palace, Bangkok, Thailand
dateDisplay: 19th century CE (cast under King Rama IV / Rama V)
medium: Cast and gilded bronze sculpture with mirrored glass inlays
creator: Royal Rattanakosin court foundry artisans
repository: In situ, Wat Phra Kaew, Grand Palace, Bangkok, Thailand
anatomy: serene princely human upper body crowned with a Thai tapering chada spire
layered gilt wings and ornate flaring avian tail-plumage
slender clawed bird legs poised on a lotus plinth
description: Standing on the upper terrace of Bangkok's Temple of the Emerald Buddha, which architecturally recreates the mythical Himavanta (Himmapan) forest at the foot of Mount Meru, this dazzling gilt-bronze Kinnorn (male Kinnara) wears a pointed Thai royal crown (chada) and jeweled breastplate above feathered bird thighs and talons. Cast by royal Siamese artisans in the 19th century, the hybrid celestial musician exemplifies Thailand's refined visual codification of Buddhist Himmapan creatures.

title: Monumental Glazed-Mosaic Yaksha Guardian (Thotsakan) at Wat Phra Kaew
originLocation: Wat Phra Kaew (Temple of the Emerald Buddha), Grand Palace, Bangkok, Thailand
medium: Brick and stucco colossal statue clad in polychrome ceramic tile and gilt glass mosaic
creator: Royal Rattanakosin court sculptors and mosaicists
repository: In situ, Wat Phra Kaew, Grand Palace, Bangkok, Thailand
anatomy: emerald-green demonic visage with bulging eyes and curling tusks
tiered multi-faced golden crown (mongkut) of the ten-headed demon king
towering armored giant body leaning on a heavy war-club (krabong)
description: Towering nearly five meters high beside a gateway of Bangkok's Temple of the Emerald Buddha, one of twelve colossal Yaksha guardians modeled on demon kings from the Thai Ramakien epic—here green-skinned Thotsakan (Ravana)—leans both hands upon his ceremonial mace. Encrusted with thousands of hand-cut polychrome porcelain and gilt-glass tesserae, the ferocious multi-tiered giant converts former mythic adversaries into tireless protectors of Thailand's sacred palladium.

title: Monumental Twin Chinthe Leogryph Guardians at the Foot of Mandalay Hill
originLocation: Southern Stairway Entrance, Mandalay Hill, Mandalay, Myanmar
dateDisplay: mid-19th century CE (c. 1857–1878, reign of King Mindon; restored 20th c.)
medium: Monumental whitewashed brick and carved stucco masonry sculpture with gilt accents
creator: Konbaung royal master masons
repository: In situ, Mandalay Hill Southern Approach, Mandalay, Myanmar
anatomy: colossal whitewashed leonine haunches and muscular chest
flaring flame-crested mane, pointed ears, and gilded trim
wide roaring fanged jaws guarding the pilgrim stairway
description: Flanking the southern covered stairway ascending sacred Mandalay Hill, twin towering whitewashed brick-and-stucco Chinthes sit upright on massive haunches with fanged jaws roaring outward over the plain. Rooted in Burmese Buddhist legend—in which a prince born of a lioness erected lion images at pagodas in remorse after slaying his grieving father—paired Chinthe guardians stand watch at virtually every monastery and stupa across Myanmar.

title: Navagunjara, the Nine-Animal Composite Manifestation of Krishna before Arjuna
originLocation: Odisha (Orissa), India
medium: Opaque watercolor and ink on layered cloth/paper (Pattachitra court idiom)
creator: Unknown Chitrakara artist of Odisha
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1998.297)
anatomy: rooster's combed head atop an arched iridescent peacock's neck
humped bull's back tapering into a slender lion's waist with a raised cobra tail
four distinct limbs: human arm holding a lotus, elephant leg, tiger paw, and deer hoof
description: Unique to the 15th-century Odia Mahabharata of poet Sarala Dasa, this 19th-century Odisha painting illustrates Krishna testing the warrior Arjuna in the forest by assuming the astonishing form of Navagunjara, an impossible creature assembled from nine distinct beings: rooster head, peacock neck, bull hump, lion waist, serpent tail, and limbs of an elephant, tiger, deer, and lotus-bearing human hand. Realizing that no natural creature could unite nine species in harmony, Arjuna drops his bow and kneels in devotion before the boundless cosmic imagination of Vishnu-Krishna.

title: Eight-Legged Winged Lion-Bird Sharabha Incarnation of Shiva
civilization: South Indian Shaiva Tradition (Mysuru / Tanjore School)
originLocation: Karnataka or Tamil Nadu, South India
medium: Opaque watercolor and gold on paper
creator: Unknown South Indian traditional painter
repository: Published historical collection (South India)
anatomy: crowned leonine-avian head with curved tusks and divine Shaiva emblems
golden feathered wings flanking a multi-armed human-lion upper body
eight powerful clawed legs capable of leaping across mountains
description: Rendered in rich South Indian polychrome and gold, this devotional painting portrays Shiva's ferocious composite avatar Sharabha—part eight-legged lion, part giant winged bird, and part multi-armed deity wielding the deer, battle-axe, snake, and fire. According to Shaiva Puranic myth and Chola-to-Mysuru temple lore, Shiva manifested as the eight-legged Sharabha to pacify the world-shaking wrath of Narasimha after Hiranyakashipu's slaying.

title: Kamadhenu (Surabhi), the Wish-Fulfilling Winged Celestial Cow beneath the Parijata Tree
originLocation: India
medium: Polychrome gouache / chromolithographic devotional print on paper
creator: Unknown 19th-century Indian devotional artist
repository: Historical Indian devotional print archive
anatomy: crowned female deity head with serene Tilaka-marked countenance
white sacred cow body containing the pantheon of Hindu gods within its flanks
polychrome feathered eagle wings and fanned peacock tail
description: Standing beneath the celestial Parijata coral-tree that emerged alongside her during the cosmic Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthan), the wish-fulfilling cow-goddess Kamadhenu displays a crowned woman's face, rainbow-feathered wings, a peacock's tail, and a sacred bovine body inhabited by the entire Hindu pantheon. Revered as the divine mother of all cattle and source of inexhaustible nourishment, her composite form visually maps the cosmos onto a single auspicious being.

title: Carved and Polychromed Sacred Wooden Mask of Barong Ket ('King of the Spirits')
originLocation: Bali, Indonesia
medium: Carved pule wood mask painted in red, black, white, and gold leaf with leather and hair attachments
creator: Unknown Balinese master mask-carver (Undagi Tapel)
repository: Wereldmuseum Amsterdam (formerly Tropenmuseum, TMnr 1116-1a-1)
anatomy: bulging round eyes and crimson leonine snout set with curved fangs

description: Carved from sacred pule wood and heightened with vermilion lacquer, gold leaf, and pierced leather ornaments, this Balinese ritual mask forms the expressive head of Barong Ket (Banaspati Raja, 'Lord of the Forest'), the lion-like protective spirit king animated by two dancers in temple courtyard performances. Locked in perpetual cosmic equilibrium against Rangda, the fanged queen of witches and leyak spirits, Barong Ket safeguards Balinese villages against pestilence and sorcery.
